subject: Tanker attacks hit a wartime high. Brent barely moved.
bodyMarkdown:
If you are filling up on the drive home from Thanksgiving dinner today, or you have a mortgage renewal coming in the spring, the same shipping lane is setting both prices. Attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz climbed to their highest level of the war in early October, and the price of oil barely budged.

## Near daily strikes, and a price that held

Reuters, citing three maritime security sources, counted at least 12 attacks on oil and gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5. The International Maritime Organization recorded 11 tankers hit while transiting Hormuz in the week ending October 4, the most since the war with Iran began in late February. USNI News described October as near daily strikes on ships. And yet Brent closed at $104.28 on October 8 after a 4 per cent jump, then slipped about 1.1 per cent to just under $104 in early Asian trading today. Kpler, the cargo tracking firm, puts shipments through the strait at roughly 10.3 million barrels a day in the week to Saturday, about 23 per cent below a prewar baseline of 13.5 million. So a quarter of the flow is gone and the price is flat. Traders have stopped pricing each attack and started pricing whether the Gulf can keep loading barrels, which so far it can.

## The G7 is speeding up barrels it already promised

On October 2 the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude and fuel through the International Energy Agency, beginning immediately over four months, with a front loaded diesel portion in the first 20 days. Read the fine print and those volumes come out of the roughly 400 million barrels already pledged under the IEA's March emergency agreement, so this is a faster schedule rather than new supply. These are **strategic reserves**, government owned stockpiles countries keep to cover a supply shock. Goldman Sachs reckons the release offsets only about half the jump in diesel prices. Reuters reported that the Trump administration had warned Germany and France to draw down diesel stocks or face American export limits, which is why one analyst called the G7 statement a political document meant to head off a US diesel export ban. The IEA's governing board met on October 7 to settle the split, and I have not seen a final allocation published.

## Where this shows up on a Canadian bill

Gasoline rose 23 per cent year over year in August and did most of the work pushing Canadian inflation to 3.0 per cent, while the Bank of Canada's preferred measures sat lower, CPI-trim at 1.9 per cent and CPI-median at 2.0 per cent. When the Bank held its rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2, it named the Middle East conflict and the Strait of Hormuz as reasons its inflation risks had moved up. That was before Canada shed 68,000 jobs in September. Diesel is the quieter problem, because it moves freight, so it reaches grocery shelves weeks later instead of the pump tonight. The **risk premium**, meaning the extra amount buyers pay for the chance supply gets cut rather than for any barrel missing today, is what keeps the Bank cautious while its own job numbers argue the other way.

## The takeaway

American September CPI lands Wednesday at 8:30 am Eastern, with the street near 3.7 per cent against 3.4 per cent in August and the Cleveland Fed's nowcast closer to 3.6, mostly energy. I would watch core, expected around 2.4 per cent, because that decides whether the Fed follows through on a December hike that FedWatch has carried above 75 per cent. Canada's own September CPI comes October 19, nine days before the Bank's October 28 decision, and a headline near 3 per cent means another hold. If you are budgeting, price diesel rather than gasoline, because freight costs arrive late and leave slowly.
